items.title: 3.8 Applying Concepts of Integration to Real-Life World Problems

source_refs.note: Book p. 115: heading 3.8 only; the printed text starts at 3.8.1 (sub-topics 3.8.1-3.8.4 on p. 115-121).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints the heading 3.8 and goes straight on to 3.8.1; there is no text of its own under this heading. This note (ours) shows how the four sub-topics fit together.
In every part of 3.8 we use one idea again and again: when a quantity is built from very many tiny pieces, we write the contribution of one small piece and then add all the pieces with a definite integral.

blocks.caption: The four applications in 3.8 (our summary)
rows: \(r^{2}\,\delta m\) for a small mass \(\delta m\) at distance \(r\)
\(C(t)\,\delta t\), concentration times a short time

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: What you need before starting: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus \(\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)\), the power rule \(\int x^{n}\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c\), and \(\int e^{kx}\,dx = \frac{e^{kx}}{k} + c\). Every example in 3.8 uses only these.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Integration adds up many small contributions; that is why it appears in physics, motion, averages and medicine.
2. First write the contribution of one small piece, then choose the limits that cover the whole body or time interval.
3. Keep the units: the unit of the answer is (unit of the integrand) \(\times\) (unit of the variable).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the limits, or using the wrong ones: the limits must cover exactly the body or the time interval in the question.
2. Dropping the units in real-life answers (kg m\(^2\), m, people, mg h/L).
